verses.note: The church fathers often read "Let Us" as a first glimpse of the Trinity. Most interpreters today agree the first readers would not have heard it that way, but many still think it fitting that the fuller revelation of Father, Son, and Spirit makes sense of the plural. The verse does not prove the doctrine; the doctrine rests on the New Testament.

The Trinitarian reading of verse 24 has an ancient history in Christian interpretation, but most modern commentators, Christian and Jewish, see a Hebrew stylistic repetition. The doctrine of the Trinity rests on the New Testament, not on this verse.

The New Testament writers keep the Shema and confess Jesus within it. Paul's ‘one God, the Father’ and ‘one Lord, Jesus Christ’ (1 Corinthians 8:6) divides the Shema's own words between Father and Son. The church's doctrine of the Trinity is a confession of the one God of this verse, not a departure from it.

Christian theology read ‘begotten’ as describing the Son's eternal relation to the Father, the language the Nicene Creed uses (‘begotten, not made’). The psalm does not state that doctrine on its own; it supplies the vocabulary of Father and Son that the fuller revelation fills.

The one addressed as God in verse 6 has a God in verse 7 who anoints him. Christian theology, following Hebrews 1:9, reads the pair as the Son addressed by the Father; Acts 10:38 speaks of God anointing Jesus with the Holy Spirit. The verse does not by itself teach the doctrine, but it is one of the Old Testament lines the early church found it could only read in that light.

The Son stands in the river, the Spirit of God descends, and in the next verse the Father speaks. The church has seen in the scene one of Scripture's clearest revelations of the one God as three persons, acting together and distinctly.

The Father speaks of the Son on whom the Spirit has come. The verse does not use the word Trinity, but it is the scene the church most often cited for the distinct persons of the one God, and Matthew's Gospel will end with the single name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (28:19).
Before the baptism scene, John already links the coming Son to the Spirit whom he will give. Mark's prologue introduces all three persons before Jesus says a word.
The Son rises from the water, the Spirit descends, and in the next verse the Father speaks. The church fathers pointed to this scene when they confessed one God in three persons.
The Father speaks to the Son on whom the Spirit has come. The New Testament does not yet use the word Trinity, but this scene became one of the church's principal witnesses to the three persons.

The Father speaks from the cloud of his presence and names Jesus as his own Son. The verse distinguishes the Father who speaks from the Son who is named, and it grounds the Son's authority to be heard in his relation to the Father, not in his standing among the prophets.

Jesus speaks of himself as sent by the Father, so that receiving him is receiving the Father. The verse teaches both the Son's distinct mission and his unity with the one who sent him, a pattern John's Gospel develops at length (John 13:20).

The Son addresses the Father as another, and yields his will to the Father's. The church confessed from this text that the Son is distinct from the Father and fully shares our humanity, including a human will, while one in being with the Father.

The Most High, his power, the Holy Spirit, and the Son of God all appear in one sentence. The verse does not state a doctrine of the Trinity, but it is one of the texts from which the church learned to speak of Father, Son, and Spirit acting together.

The Son is baptized and praying, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. The church fathers cited this scene constantly as a revelation of the three persons of the one God acting together and distinctly.

The Father speaks from the cloud of his presence about the Son before him. The scene, like the baptism, sets the Father and the Son in distinct relation while showing their unity of purpose, part of the evidence from which the church later confessed God as Father, Son, and Spirit.

The sending runs from the Father to the Son and from the Son to the disciples. Luke's Christology here is functional but high: the Son's authority is so bound up with the Father's that rejecting him is rejecting the one who sent him.

In one sentence the Son rejoices in the Holy Spirit and praises the Father. Luke shows the three persons at work in a moment of prayer, each in his own role, well before the church framed the doctrine.

The Father and the Son know one another with a knowledge no creature shares, and the Son alone can open that knowledge to others. The church later expressed this mutual knowledge in the confession of the Son as one in being with the Father (Nicaea, 325).

The verse holds two truths together that the church would later spell out as the doctrine of the Trinity: the Word is personally distinct from God the Father (with God) and shares the one divine nature (was God). Either claim without the other would deny what John says.

The relationship between the Word and God did not begin at the incarnation. It was there in the beginning, which is why the church confessed that the Son's relation to the Father is eternal, not a role he took on for a time.

The verse begins and ends the prologue's frame: the Son is God and is at the Father's side, as the Word was God and with God in verse 1. Distinction and oneness are held together at the close exactly as at the opening.
The Father who sent John speaks, the Spirit descends, and the Son is identified. The scene is one of the passages from which the church learned to confess one God in three persons.

The Father's love for the Son is the ground of the Son's authority. The relation between them is described as love before it is described as command, and the Gospel later says the Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world (17:24).

Equality with God is ascribed to the Son at the moment his distinct relation to the Father is stressed (‘his own Father’). The church's later confession held both together: the Son is fully God and is distinct from the Father as Son.

The church's doctrine of inseparable operations, that the Father, Son, and Spirit act together in every work toward creation, draws on this verse. Augustine (On the Trinity 2.1.3) and Hilary of Poitiers read the Son's dependence as his origin from the Father, not as inferiority, since what he does is whatever the Father does. Christians who debate whether the Son's submission to the Father is eternal agree that this verse denies any independent or rival divine will.

Augustine, in his Tractates on John, read this verse as describing the Father's eternal begetting of the Son: the Father gives the Son to have life in himself by begetting him, not by adding life to one who existed without it. The Nicene phrase ‘begotten, not made’ expresses this understanding. The alternative reading, that the verse describes the incarnate Son's commission, also holds that what is given is the divine life itself.

The Son's will and the Father's will are not in conflict. The fathers who defended Nicene faith, and later Maximus the Confessor in the debates of the seventh century, read such sayings as describing the Son's obedience in his human will to the one divine will he shares with the Father.

The Son has a will and freely makes the Father's will his own. The church at the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681) confessed two wills in Christ, divine and human, in harmony; texts like this one were part of that discussion.

The ‘living Father’ gives the Son to have life in himself (5:26), and the Son gives it to those who feed on him. The verse traces life from the Father through the Son to the believer, and the Nicene confession of the Son as ‘God from God, light from light’ describes the same relation of origin without inequality.

Jesus' knowledge of the Father rests on his origin from the Father: ‘I am from him’. John distinguishes the Son's coming from the Father, which belongs to who he is, from his being sent, which is his mission, and the church's later confession of the Son as eternally from the Father builds on texts like this.

The Father and the Son are two witnesses, distinct in their testimony, yet their witness is one. John does not reduce the Son to the Father's mouthpiece or make them rivals; the distinction and the unity are held together, as in 10:30 and 14:10.

The Son does nothing from himself, speaks what the Father taught, and is never left alone by the Father. John's picture of the Son's dependence is not a sign of lesser status but of perfect unity of will and action (5:19).

The Father knows the Son and the Son knows the Father with a knowledge that is mutual and complete (Matthew 11:27). The verse makes that eternal relation the pattern for the relation between Christ and his people.

The verse became one of the church's central texts for the Trinity. Tertullian (Against Praxeas 22) noted that Jesus said ‘one thing’, not ‘one person’, against those who merged Father and Son, and Augustine's Tractates on John drew the same lesson against the Arians from ‘one’ and against the Sabellians from ‘are’. The Son is distinct from the Father and one with him in being and act.

The Father in the Son and the Son in the Father describes a unity closer than cooperation: each dwells in the other. Later theology called this mutual indwelling perichōrēsis, and John 10:38, 14:10-11, and 17:21 are its main biblical ground.
The Son does the work, the Father hears and sends, and the whole action is presented as the Father's work through the Son (5:19-21). The sign reveals a relationship, not an independent wonder-worker.

The Son prays, the Father answers, and the answer is spoken for others. John shows the relationship of Father and Son in audible form, as the baptism and transfiguration do in the other Gospels (Mark 1:11, Mark 9:7).

Early Christian readers generally took the verse to mean that Isaiah saw the pre-existent Son, a reading that became part of the church's case for his full divinity. Some modern interpreters read it instead as Isaiah foreseeing the glory of Jesus' coming ministry, as Abraham is said to have seen his day (8:56).

The Father is glorified in the Son and glorifies the Son in himself. John describes a relationship of mutual honor within God, the ground for Jesus' prayer in 17:1-5 and for the church's confession that the Son shares the Father's glory.

The Father and the Son are distinct (one is in the other) and yet each is in the other. Greek theology later named this mutual indwelling perichōrēsis, and John of Damascus used the term for the persons of the Trinity in his Exposition of the Orthodox Faith in the eighth century. The verse is one of the texts on which that teaching rests.

One sentence names three agents: the Son who asks, the Father who gives, and the Advocate who is given. The church's later confession that the Spirit is a distinct person, sent by the Father at the Son's request, rests on sayings like this one.

‘We will come’ joins the Father and the Son in a single act, and verse 26 names the Spirit as the one sent in the Son's name. The Father and the Son dwell in the believer through the Spirit, so that the presence of one is the presence of all three.

The Nicene faith confesses the Son as of one being with the Father and yet not the Father, begotten of him. Read within that confession, the Father's greatness is either the priority of the source (the Father begets, the Son is begotten) or the Son's humility in the incarnation, and neither makes the Son a lesser god. How best to state the order within the Trinity is still discussed among theologians who share this confession.

The Son is loved by the Father and keeps his commands. John presents the eternal relation of the Father and the Son (17:24) as the ground of the love the disciples are invited into, so that the love between the Father and the Son is the first love of all.

The East reads the verse as distinguishing the Spirit's eternal procession from the Father, the one source (the monarchy of the Father), from his temporal sending by the Son; to say the Spirit proceeds also from the Son, Orthodox theologians have argued, confuses the persons or makes two sources in God. The West reads the verse's parallel clauses as describing the Spirit's mission, which reflects his eternal relation, and holds with Augustine that the Spirit proceeds from the Father principally and, by the Father's gift, from the Son, as from one principle, so that the Son is not a second source; it points to texts that call the Spirit the Spirit of the Son (Galatians 4:6) and to 16:14-15. Both confess the Spirit as fully God, worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son. The dispute concerns how to speak of the Spirit's origin, and whether one part of the church could add to a creed agreed by all.

The Spirit receives from the Son what the Son has from the Father. Cyril of Alexandria used these verses to argue that the Spirit belongs to the Son's own being, and Western theologians cited them in support of the filioque; Eastern theologians have answered that the verses concern what the Spirit makes known, not the origin of his being. Both readings agree that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit share one life, since all the Father has is the Son's and the Spirit declares it.

The Son's communion with the Father holds when every human companion fails. John's I am not alone stands beside Mark's cry from the cross, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34), and the church has held both: the Son truly bore abandonment and was never separated from the Father's love.

Arian writers cited the only true God to deny that the Son is true God. Nicene readers answered that the phrase distinguishes the one God from idols, not the Father from the Son, and that knowing the Son is here joined to knowing God as the content of eternal life, something no creature could be. 1 John 5:20 says of Jesus Christ that he is the true God and eternal life.

The Son had glory with the Father before the world existed. The verse teaches the Son's personal pre-existence as plainly as 1:1, and in Isaiah the LORD says he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8, 48:11), so that the Son's sharing the Father's glory places him within the identity of the one God. Some later unitarian readers took the glory as one destined for him in God's purpose, but the imperfect eichon, ‘I had’, and the phrase with you describe possession.

"All I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine" describes a complete sharing between the Father and the Son. Luke's parable has a father say to his son that all he has is his (Luke 15:31); only here is it said in both directions, which the church has read as a statement of one shared divine life.

The unity of believers is modeled on and drawn into the unity of the Father and the Son: they are to be in us. The verse does not make believers one in the way the Father and the Son are one in being, but it makes the divine communion the source and pattern of theirs.

The Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world. Love belongs to God's eternal life before creation, so that the statement that God is love (1 John 4:8) describes the relationship of the Father and the Son from eternity, not only God's attitude toward the world.

The Father sends the Son (verse 21), and the Son gives the Spirit (verse 22). Augustine cited this verse in his argument that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father (On the Trinity, book 4), a text that became part of the Western case for the filioque; Eastern theologians read it as the Son's giving of the Spirit in time, not as his eternal procession.

John calls Jesus God while distinguishing him from the Father, whom Jesus has just called ‘my God’ (verse 17). The Gospel's framing statements (1:1, 1:18, 20:28) are among the texts from which the church learned to confess one God in Father, Son, and Spirit.

The Father gives the promised Spirit to the exalted Son, and the Son pours the Spirit out on his people. The verse names all three persons and their distinct roles in a single act, which later theology would describe as the Spirit sent by the Father through the Son.

Grace and peace come jointly from the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The verse does not state a doctrine of the Trinity, but it shows the pattern of worship and prayer out of which the church later confessed the Son as one in being with the Father (compare Larry Hurtado, Lord Jesus Christ, 2003, on early devotion to Jesus).

The same Spirit is called the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ, and his dwelling in believers is the same as Christ being in them (verse 10). Western theologians from Augustine onward cited such texts in arguing that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (the filioque); Eastern Orthodox theologians answer that the verse speaks of the Spirit's sending and indwelling, not his eternal origin.
The Father raises, the Son is raised, and the Spirit is the one through whom life is given. The verse is one of several in this chapter where Father, Son, and Spirit act together in a single work.
The Father searches hearts and knows the Spirit's mind; the Spirit intercedes according to the Father's will. The verse shows a communion of knowledge and purpose between the Father and the Spirit.

The punctuation question has been decided both ways by faithful scholars. Erasmus in the sixteenth century raised doubts about the traditional reading, and the Revised Standard Version (1946) put the separate doxology in its text. Most modern translations (NIV, ESV, NRSV, BSB) read it of Christ; the committee behind the United Bible Societies' Greek text was divided, and Bruce Metzger, in a note in his Textual Commentary and in a 1973 essay, set out the case for the Christological reading, which Murray Harris also defends in Jesus as God (1992). The confession of Christ's deity does not rest on this verse alone (John 1:1, 20:28, Titus 2:13, Hebrews 1:8).

The church confesses the Son as equal with the Father and his kingdom as without end. Within that confession, the main readings of this verse are that it concerns the incarnate Son's mediatorial work, completed and handed over, or the eternal order between Father and Son in which the Son is from the Father without being less. What the church has rejected is a reading that ends the Son's reign or makes him a creature.
Grace and peace come jointly from the Father and from Jesus as Lord. Paul does not argue for Christ's divine status; he assumes it in the greeting, a way of speaking the later creeds made explicit.

The sentence moves from the Father who chooses (verses 3 to 6), through the Son who redeems (7 to 12), to the Spirit who seals (13 and 14), each section ending in praise of God's glory. The Trinitarian shape is not a formula but the structure of the praise.

Access to God is through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. The verse does not define the Trinity, but it shows that Christian prayer and worship are shaped by all three, which is part of the ground from which the doctrine grew.

The appeal rests on Christ, on love (almost certainly God's love, compare 2 Corinthians 13:14), and on the Spirit. Paul's ethics grow out of a threefold experience of God before the church had words for the doctrine.

Jesus receives the confession that Isaiah reserves for the LORD alone, and yet the confession is to the glory of God the Father. The verse holds together the Son's sharing in the one divine name and his distinction from the Father, the pattern the church later confessed as the Trinity.

The Son is distinguished from God (he is God's radiance and imprint) and yet shares God's nature so fully that to see him is to see God. The Nicene fathers used the image of light and its radiance, never separated, to explain how the Son is eternally from the Father yet equal with him.

The Father commands worship of the Son while remaining distinct from him. The verse contributes the practice of worship to the evidence behind the later doctrine: the church worshiped the Son before it had defined his relation to the Father.

The Son is addressed as God, and in the next breath God is called his God, who anoints him. The verse holds the Son's deity and his distinction from the Father together, the pairing the church later expressed in the doctrine of the Trinity.

The verse is one of the New Testament's clearest trinitarian sentences: Christ offers himself, through the eternal Spirit, to God. The whole Godhead acts in the atonement, the Son as priest and victim, the Spirit empowering, the Father receiving.
